listenings.text: I design these systems, so let me save you some time on three phrases you will hear about forty times this week. The first is API first. It sounds like a commitment and it is a description of how they built their own product, which tells you nothing about how hard it will be to connect to yours. The second is we reduce friction. Friction is real, but the word covers everything from two days of settlement delay to one extra click, and those are not the same problem or the same price. And the third is enterprise grade. That phrase has no definition. Nobody has ever failed an enterprise grade test, because there is no test. When somebody says any of the three, the useful move is the same: ask them to say the sentence again without the phrase.

A demo is a piece of theatre and I say that with affection, because I have built plenty of them. Everything you are watching was chosen. The volume is small. The data is clean. The two systems in the demo were built by the same team in the same week, which is why the integration looks effortless. None of that is dishonest, but it does mean the demo answers exactly one question, which is whether the idea works at all. It answers nothing about your volume, your data or your regulator. So the question I would ask, at the end of every demo, is very simple. What did you take out of this demo to make it run smoothly, and what would I see if you put it back in?

It is worth remembering how recent all of this is. Banks used to send payment instructions as short coded messages with very little room for information, and everybody accepted that a cross-border payment took days, because there was no alternative. Compliance teams used to work from those same thin messages, which is why so much of the checking happened by telephone. What changed was not one invention. The message format got richer, domestic systems became instant in one country after another, and suddenly the gap between what a customer experienced at home and what they experienced abroad became impossible to defend. That gap is the entire market you are walking into this week. Almost every company on that exhibition floor is selling one answer to the same question, which is why the old chain is still slower than the new domestic rails.

reading.rtitle: What They Say, and What It Commits Them To
paras: Three phrases will follow you around an exhibition floor, and none of the three means what a listener naturally assumes. Learning to hear them is not cynicism. It is the difference between a meeting that produces a decision and a meeting that produces a feeling.

The first is API first. It sounds like a promise about your project and it is a statement about their own architecture: they built their product so that everything is reachable through an interface. Useful, but it says nothing about how much work it will be to reach interoperability with a bank that runs three systems from three decades. The second is we reduce friction. The word is doing too much: it covers two days of settlement delay and it covers one extra click, and those are not the same problem, the same fix or the same price. The third is enterprise grade, which has no definition at all. Nobody has ever failed an enterprise grade test, because no such test exists.

Against those, there are phrases that do commit somebody to something, and it is worth knowing which. If a supplier tells you their throughput is four thousand transactions a second, that is a number, and a number can be tested. If they say their middleware handles the translation between formats, you can ask which formats, and the answer is either a list or it is nothing. If they say a counterparty on the other side does not need to change anything, that is a claim with a very short path to being proved wrong.

The same test applies to the compliance burden, which is where most optimistic timelines quietly die. “We are fully compliant” is a phrase, not a fact, because compliance is always compliance with something, in a named jurisdiction, at a named date. A supplier who is comfortable naming the regulation is a supplier who has met it. A supplier who moves to the next slide has just told you something.

And there is a longer memory worth carrying into these conversations. Banks used to send payment instructions as short coded messages, and everybody accepted that money took days to cross a border because there was no alternative. That is what almost every company on that floor is selling against, whether their product is token-based or not, and whether they plan to roll out in two markets or twenty. They are all answering the same question, which is why the old chain is still slower than the new domestic one.
